Researchers found each of these before an attacker did.

Each is a working exploit against a shipping product, disclosed then patched, ordered here by the kind of agent it targeted.

Comet is Perplexity’s AI browser, one that reads pages and acts for the user. Brave showed it could be hijacked by instructions hidden in a page the user simply asked it to summarize, reporting the flaw on July 25 2025 with public disclosure on August 20.

The payload sat in a Reddit comment behind a spoiler tag, so the summarize request fed that text to the model as if it were the user’s own instruction. The agent then navigated to the user’s Perplexity account, read the email on file, opened Gmail for a one-time login code, then posted both values back as a reply to the Reddit thread.

Because it acted with the user’s authenticated sessions, same-origin policy gave no protection.

**Sources:**

*   [Brave](https://brave.com/blog/comet-prompt-injection/): Brave’s own writeup, the primary technical account of the flaw.

*   [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2025/08/20/perplexity_comet_browser_prompt_injection/): news coverage of the disclosure, with the one-time-password proof of concept.

CometJacking is a second, simpler attack on the same Comet browser, disclosed by LayerX to Perplexity on August 27 2025. A single crafted link was enough to turn the browser against its user.

The payload rode inside the link’s URL query string, which Comet parsed as agent instructions rather than as a web address. The agent gathered connected Gmail, Calendar, contact data, then base64-encoded it to slip past Perplexity’s exfiltration checks before sending it to an attacker endpoint.

The encoding defeated the content filter meant to catch stolen data.

**Sources:**

*   [LayerX](https://layerxsecurity.com/blog/cometjacking-how-one-click-can-turn-perplexitys-comet-ai-browser-against-you/): the discovering firm’s walkthrough of the single-link payload.

*   [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/cometjacking-one-click-can-turn.html): news coverage of the one-click data-theft attack.

This is the research that showed a calendar invite could hijack Gemini across Google Workspace. SafeBreach researchers Or Yair, Ben Nassi, Stav Cohen disclosed it in February 2025, presenting at Black Hat USA 2025, DEF CON 33, CODE BLUE.

Malicious prompts were placed in Google Calendar invite titles, so asking Gemini about the calendar pulled the hidden text into context, then redirected the assistant. Google mitigated it in June.

The team demonstrated eight outcomes, among them opening smart-home windows, turning on a boiler, controlling lights, streaming the victim over Zoom, exfiltrating email, leaking location through a forced website visit.

**Sources:**

*   [SafeBreach](https://www.safebreach.com/blog/invitation-is-all-you-need-hacking-gemini/): the researchers’ primary account of the calendar-invite attack.

*   [Invitation Is All You Need](https://sites.google.com/view/invitation-is-all-you-need/home): the project page, with videos of the demonstrated outcomes.

*   [DEF CON 33](https://media.defcon.org/DEF%20CON%2033/DEF%20CON%2033%20presentations/Ben%20Nassi%20Or%20Yair%20&%20Stav%20Cohen%20-%20Invitation%20Is%20All%20You%20Need!%20Invoking%20Gemini%20for%20Workspace%20Agents%20with%20a%20Simple%20Google%20Calendar%20Invite.pdf): the conference presentation slides.

*   [Black Hat USA 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nmMUMzLxBkU): video of the conference talk.

*   [CODE BLUE](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WlqO2gSBE-c): video of the same talk at that security conference.

*   [Ben Nassi](https://www.nassiben.com/): the researcher’s page collecting this alongside related agent research.

The Gemini Trifecta is a set of three separate flaws Tenable found across the Gemini suite, reported around September 2025 and since fixed by Google.

Together they showed how many routes a single assistant can offer. One flaw injected instructions through logs surfaced by Cloud Assist.

A second rode in through search personalization. A third used the browsing tool as an exfiltration path.

**Sources:**

*   [Tenable](https://www.tenable.com/blog/the-trifecta-how-three-new-gemini-vulnerabilities-in-cloud-assist-search-model-and-browsing): the discovering firm’s primary report on all three flaws.

*   [Hackread](https://hackread.com/google-gemini-trifecta-vulnerabilities-gemini-ai/): news coverage summarizing Tenable’s three findings.

PleaseFix is a study showing one technique work across four different browser agents.

The Cloud Security Alliance published the research note on March 3 2026, with Zenity Labs demonstrating the same zero-click hijack on Comet, OpenAI’s Deep Research, OpenAI’s Atlas, Google’s Gemini.

Instructions rode ordinary calendar invites and emails, using natural phrases such as “take care of” or “handle this on my behalf” to trigger destructive actions, file exfiltration over file:// URIs, password-manager manipulation.

The note names the root cause as missing instruction provenance, made worse by inherited OAuth scope.

**Sources:**

*   [Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/CSA_research_note_PleaseFix_agentic_browser_exploits_20260328-csa-styled.pdf): the primary research note, covering all four browser agents.

*   [Zenity Labs](https://zenity.io/research/pleasefix-vulnerabilities): the team that demonstrated the zero-click hijack, with its scope across browser agents.

EchoLeak is widely described as the first zero-click prompt injection found in a production system. Aim Labs disclosed it against Microsoft 365 Copilot in June 2025, tracked as CVE-2025-32711.

A single crafted email carried hidden instructions, so with no click from the user, Copilot processed the message during normal operation, then leaked internal data through an automatic exfiltration path. Microsoft patched it the same month.

**Sources:**

*   [Aim Labs](https://www.aim.security/aim-labs/aim-labs-echoleak-blogpost): the discovering firm’s writeup, the primary account of the zero-click chain.

*   [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10540): the paper with the full technical analysis.

ForcedLeak is the same class of attack against a business CRM.

Noma Security reported it in Salesforce Agentforce in September 2025, rated critical and since patched.

The payload arrived through a Web-to-Lead form, so the CRM agent processed the poisoned lead later, then exfiltrated sales data to a Salesforce-trusted domain that had expired, which the researchers rebought for five dollars.

The stolen data left through a destination the system already trusted.

**Sources:**

*   [Noma Security](https://noma.security/blog/forcedleak-agent-risks-exposed-in-salesforce-agentforce): the discovering firm’s writeup, with the expired-domain detail.

*   [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/26/salesforce_agentforce_forceleak_attack/): news coverage of the Agentforce flaw.

ShadowLeak hit ChatGPT’s Deep Research agent, the mode that reads across a user’s connected accounts on its own. Radware disclosed it in September 2025, with the agent connected to Gmail, since fixed by OpenAI.

Hidden HTML instructions in an email directed the agent to gather inbox PII, then call an attacker-controlled URL. The request ran service-side on OpenAI’s own infrastructure, where egress restrictions were looser than on the client.

Unlike most cases here, the data left through open egress rather than a trusted domain.

**Sources:**

*   [The Record](https://therecord.media/openai-fixes-zero-click-shadowleak-vulnerability): news coverage of OpenAI’s fix.

*   [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/shadowleak-zero-click-flaw-leaks-gmail.html): a second news account, with the service-side egress detail.

AgentFlayer is a family of zero-click hijacks that hit enterprise agents across several vendors at once. Zenity Labs researchers Michael Bargury, Tamir Ishay Sharbat presented it at Black Hat USA 2025 in August, against agents from Microsoft, Google, OpenAI, Salesforce.

The attack needed only the target’s email address. Poisoned content reached the agent, which then collected whatever its connectors could touch, acting as a trusted adviser the attacker quietly steered.

**Sources:**

*   [Zenity Labs](https://labs.zenity.io/p/hsc25): the researchers’ writeup of the zero-click family.

*   [Black Hat USA 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M_BDq2hTJxU): video of the Zenity talk, “AI Enterprise Compromise: 0click Exploit Methods,” where these exploits were presented.

*   [Dark Reading](https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/ai-agents-access-everything-zero-click-exploit): news coverage of the cross-vendor impact.

CamoLeak turned GitHub Copilot Chat into a channel for stealing private code. Omer Mayraz of Legit Security found it in June 2025, fixed on August 14, tracked as CVE-2025-59145 at CVSS 9.6.

Instructions hid inside an HTML comment in a pull request or issue, invisible to a human reader yet read as raw text by Copilot.

The agent was redirected to search the repository for secrets, then exfiltrate them one character at a time through a prebuilt dictionary of GitHub-signed Camo image URLs, so the data left through GitHub’s own image proxy.

It stole live AWS credentials, along with the full text of an undisclosed zero-day held in a private issue.

**Sources:**

*   [Legit Security](https://www.legitsecurity.com/blog/camoleak-critical-github-copilot-vulnerability-leaks-private-source-code): the discovering firm’s writeup, with the Camo image-proxy technique.
